title: Solar farm development impacts on Eastern Box Turtle (Terrapene Carolina) Home Ranges
abstract: Eastern Box Turtle (Terrapene carolina) populations have declined drastically since 1970 because of continued destruction and fragmentation of their habitat. Although they are known to shift their home ranges because of environmental degradation, it is unknown how solar arrays impact Eastern Box Turtles. From 2011–2018, we collected data on Eastern Box Turtle movement and occupancy in a 79-ha solar farm. The solar farm is divided into six fenced areas, each containing wildlife openings for movement of terrestrial fauna every 23 m around the fenced solar arrays. We hypothesized that the solar arrays changed the home range sizes of turtles that interacted with the field. We fitted 41 Eastern Box Turtles with radio transmitters and tracked their locations twice per week in June–August from 2011–2018. Seventeen turtles had home ranges that overlapped with the solar arrays whereas 24 turtles had home ranges that never interacted with the solar arrays. We calculated home range sizes and tested for differences between overlapping and nonoverlapping groups. We further considered if the number of observations within the solar farm impacted home range size and displacement. We found that Eastern Box Turtles that used the solar farm exhibited 55–83% larger home ranges on average than turtles in natural habitats, but there was no significant association of home range size with the amount of time observed within the solar farm. Finally, we discuss strategies to mitigate negative impacts of solar farm development on turtles.

Solar Farm Development Impacts on Eastern Box Turtle (Terrapene carolina) Home Ranges

RYAN P. DOUGHERTY,[1,2] JENNIFER HIGBIE,[3] TIMOTHY GREEN,[3] AND A. Z. ANDIS ARIETTA[1] 1School of the Environment, Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut, 06511, USA 3Department of Environmental Protection, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, New York, 11973, USA ABSTRACT.—Eastern Box Turtle (Terrapene carolina) populations have declined drastically since 1970 because of continued destruction and fragmentation of their habitat. Although they are known to shift their home ranges because of environmental degradation, it is unknown how solar arrays impact Eastern Box Turtles. From 2011–2018, we collected data on Eastern Box Turtle movement and occupancy in a 79-ha solar farm. The solar farm is divided into six fenced areas, each containing wildlife openings for movement of terrestrial fauna every 23 m around the fenced solar arrays. We hypothesized that the solar arrays changed the home range sizes of turtles that interacted with the field. We fitted 41 Eastern Box Turtles with radio transmitters and tracked their locations twice per week in June–August from 2011–2018. Seventeen turtles had home ranges that overlapped with the solar arrays whereas 24 turtles had home ranges that never interacted with the solar arrays. We calculated home range sizes and tested for differences between overlapping and nonoverlapping groups. We further considered if the number of observations within the solar farm impacted home range size and displacement. We found that Eastern Box Turtles that used the solar farm exhibited 55–83% larger home ranges on average than turtles in natural habitats, but there was no significant association of home range size with the amount of time observed within the solar farm. Finally, we discuss strategies to mitigate negative impacts of solar farm development on turtles.

According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Special Report on Global Warming of 1.58C, the world has only 11 yr to drastically change its energy infrastructure and reduce global emissions to prevent the impending climate crisis (IPCC, 2018). Solar energy can provide a large portion of the energy infrastructure needed to replace fossil fuels, natural gas, coal, and nuclear energy (IPCC, 2011). As of 2018, there were 39 states in the United States that possessed utility-scale solar projects larger than 5MWAC (Bolinger et al., 2019). Additionally, total solar voltaic and concentrating solar–thermal power capacity is projected to more than double its 2018 capacity by 2024 in the United States (Bolinger et al., 2019).

Implementing renewable energy infrastructure, such as solar energy, may help slow the climate crisis and its related effects such as droughts, catastrophic floods, and ecosystem collapse (Cameron et al., 2012). On the other hand, it is also important to note the potential environmental impacts of solar fields. Land cover change because of solar infrastructure construction is garnering more attention over its impacts on local biodiversity (Lovich and Ennen, 2011; Hernandez et al., 2014). Land suitable for solar fields, such as deciduous forests or deserts, is often home to rare species or biota that perform important ecosystem functions. In 2009, one million acres of the Mojave Desert was set aside for solar field construction, which caused major conflicts with conservation groups intending to protect rare species such as Desert Tortoises (Gopherus agassizii) and FringeToed Lizards (Uma scoparia) (Woody, 2009; Lovich and Ennen, 2011), which are considered Critically Endangered and Stable, respectively, according to the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) (Hammerson, 2007; Berry et al., 2021). The solar field project was ultimately cast aside in favor of wildlife conservation. However, there were other solar projects in California that were approved, including the Ivanpah Solar Electric Generating System, which is located less than 10 miles from the Mojave National Preserve. The Environmental Impact Assessment of the project concluded that there would be

significant impacts to Desert Tortoises populations and other vulnerable biota in the area (Bureau of Land Management [BLM], 2009).

Previous studies have shown that solar arrays produce wildlife mortality and microclimate shifts because of machinery, and they impact plant composition, food availability, biodiversity, and predator makeup (Turney and Fthenakis, 2011; Hernandez et al., 2014). Given that local and federal regulations and policies have advocated against solar development in the built environment in the United States, such as skyscrapers or atop commercial infrastructure, it is likely that new solar developments will take place within natural landscapes such as scrubland, shrubland, and herbaceous environments (Hernandez et al., 2015). If this is the case, it is essential to assess the potential impacts that renewable energy development will have on and fauna.

Construction of the Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) Solar Farm (BNLSF), New York, USA, is an example of attempts made to balance the need for wildlife conservation while also providing much-needed renewable energy infrastructure to the area. The BNLSF is a 32-megawatt solar photovoltaic power plant contained in a 195-acre area that began delivering power to Long Island, New York in November 2011. At the time of construction, and during this study, it was among the largest solar farms on the east coast (BNL, 2012). In an effort to allow fauna to traverse in and out of this new facility, BNL environmental managers outfitted the fences surrounding BNLSF with wildlife openings.

To measure the effects BNLSF would have on the home ranges of Eastern Box Turtles (Terrapene carolina) native to the area, we outfitted 45 turtles with radio transmitters, and their home ranges were monitored from June 2011 to August 2018. Eastern Box Turtles are a popular species used in radio telemetry studies because of their relatively small and manageable home ranges, which makes home range area estimation easier and more accurate (Habeck et al., 2019). Additionally, the IUCN lists Eastern Box Turtles as Vulnerable with a decreasing population trend (Van Dijk, 2011). Much of this population decline is because of vehicle-related mortality, urbanization,

habitat fragmentation, ranavirus infection, and illegal pet trading (Allender et al., 2006, 2011; Kornilev et al., 2006; Ferronato et al., 2015). This makes them an important species to monitor in relation to any construction that may negatively impact their native habitat.

Conservation managers have employed different practices over the years to maintain stable turtle populations, such as translocation. Some studies suggest that translocated turtles expand their home range area and travel further than individuals in their original environment because of lack of sufficient resources, while other studies have found no difference in home range size between translocated and resident turtles (Attum and Cutshall, 2015; Henriquez et al., 2017). More akin to our investigation, studies which monitored Eastern Box Turtles in anthropogenically disturbed environments found that individuals in disturbed environments had smaller home ranges than those in undisturbed habitats (Iglay et al., 2007; Brown et al., 2021). Home range and movement decline were perceived by Iglay et al. (2007) and by Brown et al. (2021) as resulting from isolation that was caused by habitat fragmentation and overall loss in available habitat.

Given the grassland and forest habitat displaced by BNLSF, and the implementation of wildlife openings for accessible entry of terrestrial fauna, our objective was to determine the impacts of solar fields on Eastern Box Turtles by estimating movement and home ranges of individual Eastern Box Turtles within and outside of the solar fields. We hypothesized that the solar farm development would have an impact on the home range area of Eastern Box Turtles because of changes in available habitat characteristics.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

Study Site.—We conducted our study at BNL, located in Upton, Long Island, New York. The property covers 2,131 ha with approximately 688 ha developed near the center. BNL is home to BNLSF, which covers a 79-ha area on the southeastern portion of BNL. Before the solar fields were constructed, the area was composed of approximately 18 ha of grassland and farm fields and 61 ha of trees, consisting of pitch pine (Pinus rigida), various oaks (Quercus spp.), white pine (Pinus strobus), and an ericaceous understory (BNL, 2009). After the solar field construction, the floral community consisted almost entirely of successional grasses. The area surrounding the solar fields consists of mostly pine barrens habitat of pitch pine (Pinus serotina), oak species (Quercus spp.), and red maple (Acer rubrum) (BNL, 2020).

The BNLSF is divided into six fenced areas each containing 30.5-cm wide by 10.16-cm high wildlife openings located every 23 m along the solar array fencing to allow movement of terrestrial fauna (Fig. 1). Additionally, other openings occurred naturally because of uneven ground surface or holes that mammals had dug along the fences (Daub et al., unpubl. data). These openings should have allowed ample room for turtles to traverse because multiple studies have recorded mean carapace height for male and female Eastern Box Turtles to be less than 65 mm on average (Wilson and Ernst, 2005; West and Klukowski, 2016). Successional grasses between rows of solar panels within the solar fields are mowed annually during the spring to prevent overgrowth that would block sunlight. According to a BNL Sitewide Biological Inventory Report, Eastern Box Turtles are the most frequently observed reptile and are found in all sampled habitats on the property (CDM, 1995).

Fieldwork.—From 2011 to 2018, we outfitted 45 Eastern Box Turtles with radio transmitters and gave each turtle unique notch codes with v-notches filed into the marginal scutes (Cagle, 1939). We glued radio transmitters to the vertebral scutes of each turtle’s carapace with epoxy glue and replaced them every 2–3 yr depending on battery life. Turtles were tracked using a Model R1000 receiver and 3-element yagi antenna (Communications Specialist). A 64s global positioning systems (GPS; Garmin) was used to record location. Upon locating a turtle, we recorded the date, time, and GPS location (UTM with accuracy of 63 m). Each coded transmitter emits a different frequency with which individuals were identified. We tracked each turtle twice per week unless the turtle was found deceased, the transmitter stopped working, or there were unsuitable weather conditions. Each year, tracking began in early June and ended in midNovember (except in 2011 and 2012 because of lack of funding). We recorded turtle location until the end of July 2018. Transmitter data were recorded in 2018 but were withheld from home range estimation because of small sample size.

From June to the end of July, 2015–2017, we chose 8 of the 45 turtles to be tracked twice per day (Monday to Friday) using the same methods. Turtles were chosen randomly to represent home ranges overlapping with the solar farm and different areas of BNL not related to BNLSF. During the remainder of each season, these eight turtles were tracked at the same frequency as others. Data were removed for turtles monitored twice per day if the number of days between monitoring turtle locations exceeded eight (because of bad weather events or a lag between the end of fall and start of spring the following year) or if locations were repeated in the winter because of overwintering.

Home Range Estimation.—We divided turtles into two condition groups based on their relation to the solar fields: 1) turtles whose home range intersected the solar fields (SF; n = 17), and 2) turtles who had no interaction with the solar fields (NOSF; n = 24). Four turtles were omitted from home range analysis because of having missing data, outliers, and only 1 yr of data. We excluded all years per individual turtle from analysis when turtles were observed fewer than 10 times during the tracking season. We did not test home range size against sex because a disproportionate number of Eastern Box Turtles used in the study were females (33 females, 8 males) and the sex bias was consistent across groups (SF: 14 females, 3 males; NOSF: 19 females, 5 males) (Appendix 1). Straight-line distances were measured between the original location each turtle was found and its final transmitted location (net displacement) to assess the overall shift of home ranges between the two groups.

Data were analyzed with R using the package adehabitatHR (Calenge, 2006; R Core Team, 2016) and ArcGIS, Environmental Systems Research Institute (ESRI, 2011). We used minimum convex polygons (MCP) and kernel utilization distribution (K95%) models, with a least-square cross-validation smoothing parameter, at the 95% isopleth, to compute the area within each turtle’s home range. The K95% uses a bivariate probability density function to give the probability density to relocate the animal at any place according to its coordinates (Calenge, 2006). The MCP was used in addition to K95% because it is the most commonly used home range estimator for Eastern Box Turtles (Henriquez et al., 2017; Habeck et al., 2019).

Statistical Analyses.—All statistical analyses were completed in R (R Core Team, 2016). We assessed the normality of our data with a Shapiro-Wilk test. In order to avoid pseudoreplication, each turtle’s home range area was averaged by the number of

years it had been tracked because the area of one year’s home range data would inform the following year’s home range data.

To test for difference in home range size, we fit linear models with the log-transformed home range as response for both MCP and K95% methods and tested for a difference in home ranges between conditions (SF vs. NOSF). Home range observations were uneven across individuals (nObservation = 147, nIndividual = 41); we accounted for this with a mixed model framework treating individual turtles as a random intercept (repeated measures design). We assessed statistical significance of the model parameters by estimating 95% confidence intervals with 1,000 nonparametric bootstrap iterations.

In an effort to determine if the solar fields changed turtle habitat enough for them to relocate their home range, the MCP centroid (the central coordinate of an MCP) was calculated using ArcGIS for 19 turtles (SF = 8, NOSF = 11) with more than 3 yr of tracking data (ESRI, 2011). The distance between centroids of consecutive tracking years was then summed. Given that many turtles were not tracked through 2018 because of death or lost trackers (Appendix 1), the calculation was standardized to four consecutive years of distance between centroids. Data were taken from turtles tracked between 2013– 2017; 2013 data were only used if turtles were not monitored

consecutively from 2014–2017 (i.e., turtle was found dead or transmitter stopped working in 2017).

To further analyze the impact of solar fields on turtles’ home range sizes, we asked whether the amount of time an SF turtle spent in the solar field per year was associated with its home range size. We grouped all turtles who had years where their home range both did and did not overlap with the solar fields to find out whether home range size was different between years seen in the solar fields and years never seen in the solar fields. We fit similar repeated measures linear mixed models predicting log-transformed home ranges as with our first model, which predicted the difference in home ranges between conditions, but we treated the proportion of time each turtle was in the solar fields per year (observations in SF/total observations) as the independent variable in the model (nObservation = 60, nIndividual = 17).

Tracking.—The number of turtles recorded per season varied with year of study because of tracking inconsistency, being tagged after 2011, mortality, and/or transmitter failure (2011: n = 6, 2012: n = 22, 2013: n = 26, 2014: n = 25, 2015: n = 24, 2016: n =

FIG. 2. Tracking duration and time lag between observations for each Eastern Box Turtle. Tracking conducted between November and April was done to verify that turtles were overwintering.

23, 2017: n = 21, mean = 21). We tracked most turtles in both SF and NOSF groups for more than 3 yr (mean: SF = 3.53, NOSF = 3.62). There were eight turtles tracked for only 1 yr. Between 2011 and 2017, we recorded 5,580 individual tracking observations with a mean of 37.96 6 25.36 tracking observations per turtle during a tracking season (range = 10–118; this and all means are reported with 6SD). The SF turtles’ average proportion of total observations in the solar fields was 0.073 6 0.072 (observations in SF/total observations). Tracking duration and frequency breakdown for each turtle can be found in Figure 2. There were individual years where SF turtles were not tracked inside the solar fields. On average, SF turtles were found in the solar fields 26.1% of the years they were tracked. Of the years where SF turtles were definitively witnessed in the solar fields, the range of proportion of observations in the solar fields over total observations was 0.012–0.40 (mean = 0.106 6 0.109).

Home Range Size.—The home range area data were not normally distributed (Shapiro-Wilk test, MCP: W = 0.82356, P < 0.001; K95%: W = 0.53042, P < 0.001). Over the entire study, individual turtle home ranges measured with MCP ranged from 0.307 to 40.88 ha (mean: 5.96 6 6.77 ha). SF turtles had an average home range of 7.41 6 5.53 ha while the NOSF group had a smaller average home range of 4.57 6 3.78 ha. Home ranges measured with the kernel utilization distribution ranged from 0.085 to 48.15 ha (mean: 4.39 6 6.31 ha). The SF turtles’ average home range was 7.62 6 10.89 ha while NOSF turtles’ average home range was 4.00 6 4.53 ha.

Results of linear mixed models indicate that SF turtles’ home ranges were larger than those of NOSF turtles (Fig. 3). On average, according to the MCP model, individuals that did not interact with the solar farm exhibited an average home range size of 2.73 ha[2] (95% CI = 2.24–3.32) while SF individuals’ home ranges were 83% larger (4.98 ha[2] ) on average (95% CI = 4.00– 6.19) (Table 1). The observed increase in home ranges equates to

a 0.60 SD increase relative to NOSF turtles. The K95% mixed model estimates for NOSF turtle home ranges are slightly smaller at 1.98 ha[2] (95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.58–2.49). The K95% model estimates that home ranges of SF turtles were 55% larger (3.07 ha[2] ) than those of NOSF turtles (95% CI = 2.49– 4.26). With the K95% estimator, this equates to SF turtles having expanded home ranges that were 0.24 SDs higher relative to NOSF turtles.

Home Range Displacement.—Annual home ranges of individual turtles shifted in size and location over the years tracked. Fouryear centroid distance summation ranged from 88.97 to 693.14 m (mean = 283.5 6 167.1) among all turtles. The SF turtles (n = 8) had a mean centroid distance summation of 343.1 6 204.4 m, and NOSF (n = 11) turtles’ mean centroid distance summation was 240.2 6 127 m. The mean summed centroid distance was found to be similar between SF and NOSF turtles. There was no significant difference in the summed centroid distances over 4 yr between the two groups (F1,17 = 1.838, P = 0.193).

Home Range by Proportional Use.—The second set of linear mixed models focused on turtles which had one or more tracking seasons with home ranges that overlapped with the solar fields and those that did not overlap with the solar fields. Our models predict that home range size increased by 30% (MCP, 95% CI = -7.3–466.1) or 168% (K95, 95% CI = -1.1–3,804.6) for every 10% increase in proportion of observations in the solar field. However, confidence intervals overlapped with zero for both models (Table 2).

We hypothesized that the solar farm development has had an impact on the home range area of Eastern Box Turtles because of the change in habitat characteristics by the BNLSF. Our results suggest that human development impacts the home range size

However, both MCP and K95% home range averages were larger for SF turtles, supporting our hypothesis that turtles using developed habitat maintained larger home ranges (Table 1). Although the centroid distance results were higher on average for SF turtles (Appendix 1), they do not indicate that Eastern Box Turtle home ranges shifted more because of BNLSF implementation. The difference in centroid distance between treatments was nonsignificant. However, our results do suggest that Eastern Box Turtle home ranges are not static. Over a 4-yr period, most turtles shifted their MCP centroid by more than 200 m, while 4 of 19 turtles shifted their centroid more than 400 m. In previous studies, Eastern Box Turtles have been found to shift habitat use across seasons (Aall, 2011; Fredericksen, 2014) while, across successive years, this pattern has been observed for Wood Turtles (Glyptemys insculpta) (Hagani et al., 2021).

It is important to note that no Eastern Box Turtle home range existed entirely in BNLSF during any tracking season, and that the highest proportion of observations seen per tracking season in the solar fields was only 0.40 (mean = 0.106 6 0.109). One potential explanation could be that the 23-m fenced gaps between 30.5-cm wide wildlife openings may be inadequate entrance spaces for turtles. The NOSF turtles that had home ranges near the solar field fences either never walked along the fence far enough to find a gate or did not understand that it was an entrance. If they could not find a gate, their home range may have been restricted by the fence, thus decreasing home range area (Stickel, 1950). However, as stated in the methods, because these fenced gaps were constructed with adequate space for turtle entry, it is more likely that the proportion of time SF turtles spent inside the solar farms is reflective of their habitat preference behavior.

Box turtles are known to utilize a variety of habitats within a single year, often oscillating between relative inactivity in shaded environments in response to high temperatures and droughts in the summer and increased activity with the onset of precipitation and cooler climates (Dodd, 2001; Aall, 2011; Fredericksen, 2014). Spending most of their time in forested habitat (Dodd, 2001; Fredericksen, 2014, Parlin et al., 2017), when given the option between early successional grass/ shrubland or late successional forests, resident Eastern Box Turtles favor forests (Williams and Parker, 1987; Henriquez et al., 2017). Eastern Box Turtles generally select microhabitats that maintain their body temperature at a range of 29–38 8C (Ernst et al., 1994), above which turtles may shift habitats to seek shade or enter waterbodies to facilitate thermoregulation (Donaldson and Echternacht, 2005; Fredericksen, 2014). results, Parlin et al. (2017) found that in relation to all other habitats, the proportion of observations in grassland and herbaceous environments was only 0.074 (CI: 0.057–0.091). Fredericksen (2014) found that during May, turtles were more likely to be in edge habitats, but as temperatures increased they preferred closed-canopy forests and became less active unless there was a period of precipitation. Selection of field habitat remained relatively stable throughout all seasons at 15–22% and, importantly, females were found nesting in field sites characterized with grasses and dense layers of hardwood sprouts (Fredericksen, 2014). The habitat description provided by Fredericksen (2014) most closely resembles that of our own habitat at BNLSF. Eastern Box Turtles can extend their home range size by 400–700 m in search of adequate nesting grounds (Stickel, 1989). Therefore, it is possible that females used the solar fields as nesting sites, which could explain why SF turtles had slightly larger home ranges than those that did not use the solar

Although some individual studies have found that there is no difference in home range size between male and female Eastern Box Turtles (Dodd, 2001; Aall, 2011), a metanalysis addressing the question determined that females have a 27% larger home range on average compared to males (Habeck et al., 2019). The difference in home range size between sexes should not have significantly impacted our own results because most turtles were female and the few males that we tracked were almost evenly divided between NOSF (n = 5) and SF groups (n = 3). Conversely, Eastern Box Turtle habitat selection behavior may not differ between the sexes (Roe et al., 2018) unless it specifically relates to nest selection (Fredericksen, 2014).

Given the relative lack of solar field facilities in northeastern United States, our study is among the first to measure wildlife impacts on native species. So far, because of its status as a keystone species and the proclivity to construct utility-scale solar facilities in desert habitats, desert tortoises have been wellstudied with regard to solar farm impacts on a species and its habitat (Lovich and Ennen, 2011; Agha et al., 2020). Agha et al.’s (2020) review on solar and wind development impacts on habitat conservation, with a case study on desert tortoises, found that many species, including desert tortoises, are affected by solar development and operation. Current research indicates that the largest impacts of utility scale solar developments on desert tortoises are habitat fragmentation by roads, habitat loss, and direct mortality, all of which are linked to population

declines (Lovich and Ennen, 2011). In 2017, 256.4 km[2] of desert tortoise habitat in the Western Mojave and Ivanpah Valley deserts were classified as degraded from their previous status report in 2009. Solar and wind development was the cause of 62.6% of those habitat downgrades (Parker et al., 2018).

Considering the known impacts of solar development on desert landscapes, we might suppose similar impacts on forested landscapes. There are many factors that have been documented to affect home range size in turtles, including protection from the elements, food access, precipitation levels, available nesting sites, and proximity to other individuals (Dodd, 2001; Donaldson and Echternacht, 2005; Brown et al., 2021). Iglay et al. (2007) and Brown et al. (2021) found that turtles in more-disturbed environments moved less, or had smaller home ranges, than turtles with open and less-fragmented environments. Therefore, habitat fragmentation produces isolation that makes movements among habitats more difficult and, depending on the type of anthropogenic disturbance, more dangerous (Nazdrowicz et al., 2008). Both Iglay et al. (2007) and Brown et al. (2021) suggested that differences in movement according to sex were related to female nesting requirements. In the case of the Brown et al. (2021) study, even some female turtles outside the disturbed zone utilized it for a brief period, potentially for nesting because of the loosened soil in the construction site. In contrast, the home ranges of our turtles that interacted with BNLSF were larger than those that did not. This indicates that wildlife openings were indeed suitable for entry and exit of the solar fields and, more importantly, did not restrict movements that would result in isolation and cause emigration issues (Iglay et al., 2007; Brown et al., 2021).

Another serious problem for utility-scale solar developments is direct mortality of wildlife. Unless they are relocated, tortoises and turtles can be crushed when areas are leveled with construction equipment. Multiple studies analyzing various avenues of human disturbance on Eastern Box Turtles discovered turtles leveled by machinery, buried by road construction, or killed via vehicle collision and lawn mowing (Nazdrowicz et al., 2008; Farnsworth and Seigel, 2013). In fact, two turtles in our study were lost because of BNL maintenance work that was not associated with BNLSF, and one was killed inside a solar field by a lawnmower. Unfortunately, research has indicated that turtle relocation is not a completely viable solution to the construction problem. Relocating turtles has been shown to

increase turtle home range size, average distance traveled, and mortality rate (Hester et al., 2010; Farnsworth and Seigel, 2013).

We found that turtles using the solar fields exhibited larger home ranges than those that did not. However, due to the limitations of our study, further research needs to be conducted to determine what resources Eastern Box Turtles use within the solar fields and whether or not this habitat is less conducive for their survival. It is possible that the solar fields provide adequate nesting grounds for females and, potentially, a reliable source of shade for thermoregulation under the panels during the summer. Although we do not know the exact effects of solar development on Eastern Box Turtle survival, there is clear evidence of the harmful effects of general development on their survival (Dodd and Dreslik, 2008; Nazdrowicz et al., 2008). It is therefore imperative that developers make decisions with wildlife conservation as a main concern, including any new renewable energy developments. Large swaths of deciduous forest should be a last resort for new development, not only because forests provide vital habitat for vulnerable species such as amphibians and reptiles, but also because of the immediate carbon sequestration and biomass loss caused by deforestation (Schulp et al., 2008). There are less-ecologically deleterious options such as manipulating cityscapes. The photovoltaic electricity production potential is massive within city and suburban rooftops, and only a fraction of potential city-wide photovoltaic capacity has been reached in most cities (Kouhestani et al., 2019). Specifically in the United States, 82% of buildings <5,000 m[2] are suitable for photovoltaic solar energy while 99% of buildings larger than that are suitable. Taking full advantage of unused rooftops for solar development has the potential of offsetting 100% of household energy use in the northeast (Gagnon et al., 2018), thereby protecting vulnerable species such as Eastern Box Turtles and Desert Tortoises from further harm. Given that solar power is meant to be a sustainable alternative to protect the planet from long-term ecological destruction, the short-term impacts of its implementation should also be considered.
